value.overview: The Kelp Gull (Larus dominicanus) is a large, powerful coastal gull of the Southern Hemisphere. It is best known from the coasts of South America, southern Africa, Australia, New Zealand, and subantarctic islands. Adults have a black back and wings, white head and underparts, a strong yellow bill with a red spot, and greenish-yellow legs. The species is an adaptable scavenger and predator that uses natural shorelines as well as ports, fishing areas, and other human-modified coastal sites.
value.classification: The Kelp Gull belongs to the gull family Laridae and the order Charadriiformes. It is also called the Dominican Gull or Southern Black-backed Gull.
value.identification: This is a large gull with a broad, heavy bill and long wings. Adults have a white head, neck, underparts, and tail, contrasting with a dark slate to black back and upper wings. The wingtips are black with limited white markings. The bill is yellow with a conspicuous red spot near the tip, and the legs are usually greenish-yellow. Immature birds are mottled brown and white, with a dark bill and a dark tail band. Its size and dark back help separate it from most gulls in Central America.
value.rangeHabitat: Kelp Gulls breed mainly along rocky and sandy coasts, offshore islands, estuaries, and sheltered coastal wetlands across much of the Southern Hemisphere. They forage in the intertidal zone, shallow marine waters, beaches, river mouths, harbors, fishing grounds, and refuse sites. In Costa Rica, the species is not a regular resident or established breeder. It is an extremely rare vagrant: the first documented national record was a second-cycle bird photographed on 8 January 2013 at the mouth of the Colorado River in Barra del Colorado, Limón, on the Caribbean coast.
value.migrationStatus: The species is generally resident or locally dispersive, although some populations make seasonal coastal movements. In Costa Rica it is an accidental, exceptionally rare visitor rather than a regular migrant. The documented records are from the Caribbean coast, and there is no reliable evidence of a recurring seasonal passage or breeding population in the country.
value.breeding: Kelp Gulls usually breed colonially or in loose groups on coastal islands, rocky shores, cliffs, dunes, and other sites that offer protection from terrestrial predators. The nest is a shallow scrape or a simple structure made from vegetation and other available material. Both adults defend the nesting territory and share incubation and chick-rearing duties. Clutches commonly contain two or three eggs. Chicks are downy, mobile soon after hatching, and remain dependent on the adults while they grow.
value.dietFeeding: Kelp Gulls are opportunistic omnivores. They take fish, squid, crabs, mollusks, other marine invertebrates, carrion, eggs, and young birds. They forage by walking along beaches, probing among rocks and seaweed, swimming, dipping from the surface, and scavenging around fishing boats and ports. They may also eat discarded food and refuse. Their strong bill allows them to tear flesh and handle relatively large or tough prey.
value.behavior: This gull is alert, social, and highly adaptable. Individuals often rest or roost in groups but may defend feeding and nesting territories. They are strong fliers and commonly patrol shorelines, estuaries, and fishing areas. Kelp Gulls use a wide range of calls, including loud alarm and contact notes. They can steal food from other birds, follow boats, and exploit temporary concentrations of prey, while breeding adults vigorously defend nests and chicks.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not reliably quantified. Available information does not indicate a level of decline that currently qualifies the species for a threatened category.
